what.text: Glycine is the simplest amino acid (also called aminoacetic acid). Under US law, a product containing an amino acid and meant to supplement the diet can be sold as a dietary supplement.

what.text: Which Adonis products contain it: glycine is an added ingredient in the sermorelin + glycine tablet taken by mouth, and in some compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide injections. Adonis does not carry glycine on its own.

In rats, glycine taken by mouth increased non-REM sleep and lowered core body temperature. The study traced this to NMDA receptors in the brain’s body-clock center (the suprachiasmatic nucleus). This has not been shown in people.
There is little research on glycine for sleep, and none on glycine added to a sermorelin tablet or to a GLP-1 injection.

research.text: Human research on glycine and sleep is small. A 2026 scoping review found 3 trials of glycine supplements on sleep-related outcomes. The one we could open is described below.

research.title: Daytime sleepiness after short sleep, 2012 (Japan)

facts.v: randomized, single-blind crossover: glycine or placebo before bed, after sleep was cut by 25% for three nights
10 healthy men aged 30 to 61, all Ajinomoto employees; 7 were analyzed (1 dropped out, 2 excluded for taking medicine)
next-day sleepiness and fatigue (rating scales, questionnaire) and computer performance tests

research.found: Fatigue scores were lower and sleepiness tended to be lower with glycine. One of the computer tests (psychomotor vigilance) improved. Sleep itself was not recorded. The authors work for Ajinomoto, which makes amino acids; the paper declares no conflicts of interest.

research.text: The scoping review reported that all 3 glycine sleep trials found a benefit on at least one sleep-related outcome, and called for larger trials with standard sleep measures.

src.label: Fan et al., J Diet Suppl, 2026 (scoping review)

us.text: Glycine is not an FDA-approved drug for sleep. It can be sold as a dietary supplement, is permitted as a food additive for limited uses, and FDA-approved as a drug only as an irrigation fluid used during urologic surgery. As of October 31, 2026.

items.text: FDA no longer regards glycine as generally recognized as safe (GRAS) for human food. It is allowed as a food additive for listed uses, such as masking saccharin’s aftertaste in beverages, and as a nutrient amino acid.

after.text: Glycine is not listed on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List or the 2027 list.

side.text: There is little safety data on glycine taken for sleep. The 2012 sleep study does not report side effects.

items.text: FDA withdrew glycine’s GRAS status for human food, citing reports of adverse effects when high levels were given in the diets of experimental animals, and rising human intake.

items.text: the 2012 crossover study (7 men analyzed) did not report adverse events.

unconfirmed: Two earlier Japanese glycine sleep studies (Inagawa 2006 and Yamadera 2007, Sleep and Biological Rhythms) are not in PubMed and the journal pages could not be opened, so they are not reported.
A 2006 high-dose glycine safety study in volunteers (Seikatsu Eisei) could not be opened.
Glycine's status in Canada, the UK, the EU and Australia was not checked.
How much glycine the Adonis sermorelin tablet or GLP-1 injections contain is not on file.
surprises: Glycine is often called GRAS, but FDA's rule (21 CFR 170.50) says FDA no longer regards glycine as GRAS for human food; it is allowed only under specific food-additive rules.
Glycine is an FDA-approved drug ingredient, but only as a surgical irrigation fluid for prostate surgery and as an OTC antacid ingredient, not for sleep.
